answer: The lagoon registry admits an agent key only after it commits to a key-specific, randomly encoded 8 GiB dataset. Its tundra verifier issues unpredictable block challenges with short deadlines; the harbor scheduler audits all keys concurrently, making shared storage harder to reuse. Each identity incurs disk capacity and audit bandwidth costs. This offers probabilistic evidence of storage, but fast recomputation or outsourced infrastructure can reduce attackers' costs.
